### C-R1-01
**Claim:** Provan reads 1 Kgs 1–2 not as a true beginning of Kings but as the last chapter of the larger David story in Samuel, resolving how Nathan’s dynastic promise (2 Sam 7) can be fulfilled after the judgment and wreckage of 2 Sam 11–18.
**Quote:** "The narrative that begins our book (1 Kgs. 1–2) is really not a beginning at all, but the last chapter of the larger story of David, which is found in 1–2 Samuel."
**Locus:** §1 / 1 Kgs 1:1–53 (intro) / slice ~l.12
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[succession-narrative]], [[david]], [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]]

### C-R1-02
**Claim:** Provan takes the Abishag episode as signaling to the court (and Adonijah) that David has lost virility and thus ability to govern; the juxtaposition of sexual non-knowledge and “I will be king” makes the coup opportunistic.
**Quote:** "the importance of the Abishag incident lies in its indication to the watching court (and to Adonijah in particular) that David has lost his virility and thus his ability to govern."
**Locus:** §1 / 1 Kgs 1:1–5 / slice ~l.14
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[david]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-03
**Claim:** Provan associates Adonijah with Absalom (and Saul) via handsomeness, chariots/horses, and parental negligence, hinting that succession will not run through the Hebron-born sons but a Jerusalem-born son.
**Quote:** "In associating Adonijah so clearly with his brother, the authors have already hinted to us that this son, too, is heading for disaster. The succession will not be through any of the sons born in Hebron at all… but through one of the sons born in Jerusalem."
**Locus:** §1 / 1 Kgs 1:5–6 / slice ~l.16
**Targets:** [[succession-narrative]], [[solomon]], [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-04
**Claim:** Provan explains the Adonijah/Solomon party split partly as Hebron/Judean-past vs Jerusalem/united-kingdom present (Joab, Abiathar vs Nathan, Zadok, Shimei), to be read in light of Judah–Israel tensions that will explode again in 1 Kgs 12.
**Quote:** "It seems likely… that their support for Adonijah represents at least in part a commitment to history and tradition and to the continuing influence of Judeans at the centers of power."
**Locus:** §1 / 1 Kgs 1:7–10 / slice ~ll.18–19
**Targets:** [[succession-narrative]], [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-05
**Claim:** Provan treats David’s “oath” to Bathsheba as of unclear status—unmentioned in Samuel, not cited by Nathan to David—and may be little more than “pillow-talk,” yet it becomes the peg for Nathan and Bathsheba’s coordinated, carefully independent-looking advocacy.
**Quote:** "Is the “oath” anything more than pillow-talk between David and Bathsheba? Perhaps not… the oath has now become the slender peg upon which Nathan and Bathsheba have hung their hopes for the future."
**Locus:** §1 / 1 Kgs 1:11–27 / slice ~ll.21–22
**Targets:** [[succession-narrative]], [[solomon]], [[david]]

### C-R1-06
**Claim:** Provan contrasts Solomon’s public anointing (mule, oil, music, popular acclaim at Gihon) with Adonijah’s private elite feast as the text’s normative vs aberrant path to kingship.
**Quote:** "This is the proper way to become a king, the text tells us: out in the open, with mules, oil, and music, with popular involvement. Adonijah’s attempted coup, by stealth and patronage, is an aberration."
**Locus:** §1 / 1 Kgs 1:28–40 / slice ~l.24
**Targets:** [[kingship-in-israel]], [[solomon]], [[succession-narrative]]

### C-R1-07
**Claim:** Provan notes Adonijah’s asylum at the altar horns as shared ANE/Israelite shrine-asylum custom (Exod 21:12–14), but flags that Solomon will later ignore convention when it suits him (Joab).
**Quote:** "There is evidence within the OT that the Israelites shared the common ancient Near Eastern custom in regard to asylum at shrines (Exod. 21:12–14). As Joab will discover, however, Solomon is not beyond ignoring convention if it suits his purposes."
**Locus:** §1 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 1:49–53 / slice ~l.71
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[succession-narrative]]

### C-R1-08
**Claim:** Provan reads David’s charge (2:1–4) as defining royal strength within Mosaic/Deuteronomic law; deuteronomic language recurs throughout Kings as the measure by which Solomon and later kings are weighed and found wanting.
**Quote:** "Particularly in view here (as in Joshua) is the law code of Deuteronomy… It is deuteronomic language such as this that we shall find recurring throughout Kings, as first Solomon himself (1 Kgs. 11) and then all the succeeding kings of Israel and Judah are weighed in relation to the Mosaic law code and found wanting."
**Locus:** §2 / 1 Kgs 2:1–4 / slice ~l.94
**Targets:** [[david]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-09
**Claim:** Provan records a live tension in Kings between conditional and unconditional Davidic promise: David in 2:4 makes dynasty depend on obedience, though 2 Sam 7:14–15 sounds unconditional and some Kings texts (11:36; 15:4; 2 Kgs 8:19) echo that; exile ends monarchy yet a king remains in Babylon (2 Kgs 25:27–30).
**Quote:** "There is thus a degree of tension in Kings as to precisely what the implications of the Davidic promise are… Is the promise really dead and God’s grace wholly constrained by law? Or is there yet hope that grace will triumph over human sin and folly?"
**Locus:** §2 / 1 Kgs 2:4 / slice ~l.96
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-10
**Claim:** Provan rejects Nelson’s redactional resolution that “Israel” in 2:4 / 8:25 / 9:4–5 means only the northern kingdom; “throne of Israel” denotes the united kingdom in 8:20 and 10:9—final-form tension must be lived with.
**Quote:** "This is an unlikely hypothesis… It seems that we must simply live with the tension and seek to understand what the final form of the text, which has both these conditional and unconditional elements in it, has to say to us."
**Locus:** §2 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 2:4 / slice ~l.134
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[iain-provan]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-11
**Claim:** Provan doubts blood-guilt as David’s real motive for ordering Joab’s death: David long tolerated Joab (including Uriah), Abner/Amasa cases are ambiguous, and timing points to Joab as too dangerous a man of the Judean past/Adonijah party for Solomon’s united kingdom.
**Quote:** "All in all, then, it is difficult to believe that blood-guilt is the real reason why loyal Joab is now, at this late date, to be done away with… He is too much a man of the Judean past… He must therefore be removed, and the issue of blood-guilt becomes simply a convenient justification for his death."
**Locus:** §2 / 1 Kgs 2:5–6 / slice ~ll.104–106
**Targets:** [[david]], [[solomon]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-12
**Claim:** Provan reads 2:5–9 as carefully structured: Joab (southern disruptor) and Shimei (northern/Saulide disruptor) flank Barzillai (Transjordan model of dutiful service at the king’s table)—an ideal of peaceful community and a program of removals for Solomon.
**Quote:** "Between these two disruptive elements from Judah and Israel (2:5–6; 2:8–9) stands Barzillai from Gilead in Transjordan (2:7): a model of dutiful service… The passage is thus most carefully structured so as to present Solomon with an ideal (peaceful community) and to suggest to him what kind of people… must be removed."
**Locus:** §2 / 1 Kgs 2:5–9 / slice ~l.108
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[david]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-13
**Claim:** Provan stresses that David’s “deal according to your wisdom” means subtlety—find justification to remove Joab/Shimei; Solomon’s ḥoḵmâ will be praised later but never again used “to such ruthless effect as it is in ch. 2.”
**Quote:** "The emphasis is upon subtlety. Solomon must not act rashly, but use his brain and find some justification for removing Joab from the scene… There will be great emphasis on Solomon’s wisdom (ḥoḵmâ) in the following chs.… but it will never again be used to such ruthless effect as it is in ch. 2."
**Locus:** §2 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 2:6, 9 / slice ~l.136
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-14
**Claim:** Provan structures 2:12–46 around ḵwn (“established”): God’s establishing of Solomon (alluding to 2 Sam 7) is the presupposition of the executions, not their result—predestined success under divine sovereignty, even amid ruthless politics.
**Quote:** "While in one sense, then, these verses concern the consolidation of Solomon’s position… in another sense his security is never in doubt. He is predestined to succeed by the God who is “sovereign over the kingdoms of men”…"
**Locus:** §3 / 1 Kgs 2:12–46 (intro) / slice ~l.164
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[succession-narrative]]

### C-R1-15
**Claim:** Provan leaves Adonijah’s request for Abishag and Bathsheba’s transmission of it ambiguous (innocent vs claim-to-throne; naive vs calculating), but Solomon chooses to read it as revival of the ch. 1 conspiracy and executes—the first casualty of Solomon’s “wisdom,” someone David had not named.
**Quote:** "The first casualty of Solomon’s “wisdom” is thus, paradoxically, someone that David had not even mentioned to him and, if past events are any guide, would certainly not have wanted dead."
**Locus:** §3 / 1 Kgs 2:12–25 / slice ~ll.166–168
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[succession-narrative]], [[david]]

### C-R1-16
**Claim:** Provan judges Solomon’s blood-guilt rhetoric over Joab specious: Joab and Abiathar are condemned by association; Abiathar’s ark-carrying mitigation is weak; Joab is killed at the altar because he is a threat, not because of moral purification of David’s house.
**Quote:** "Yet obviously we must take Solomon’s rhetoric in verses 31–33 with a pinch of salt. Joab is not being killed because of Solomon’s overwhelming desire to clear David’s house of the guilt of innocent blood… He is being killed because he is a threat to Solomon and the united kingdom."
**Locus:** §3 / 1 Kgs 2:26–35 / slice ~ll.170–172
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david]]

### C-R1-17
**Claim:** Provan notes that in ordering Joab’s execution *beside* the altar Solomon himself breaks Exod 21:12–14 (murderer to be taken from the altar), while treating Shimei vindictively by the letter of a contrived boundary law.
**Quote:** "in ordering his execution beside the altar, Solomon himself is guilty of breaking the law. Exodus 21:12–14 quite clearly states that a murderer is to be taken away from the altar and put to death… Solomon’s willingness to ignore the letter of the law when it suits him only throws into sharper relief his vindictive treatment of Shimei."
**Locus:** §3 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 2:31 / slice ~l.208
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R1-18
**Claim:** Provan reads Shimei’s confinement and execution (west to Gath, not across Kidron) as Solomon seizing a technical opportunity; overall 1–2 is “a fairly sordid story of power-politics thinly disguised as a morality tale.”
**Quote:** "What we have here, in fact, is a fairly sordid story of power-politics thinly disguised as a morality tale. So tortured are the attempts to convince us that the men who died did so because they deserved it… that we cannot but be aware of their speciousness."
**Locus:** §3 / 1 Kgs 2:36–46 / slice ~ll.174–176
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[david]]

### C-R1-19
**Claim:** Provan’s theological resolution: if God ordains Solomon’s dynasty, it is not because David’s house is innocent (Solomon’s 2:31–33 implication) but because election and grace deal with their guilt; conditionality is only part of the Davidic promise story.
**Quote:** "If God has truly ordained that Solomon should be king and have a dynasty, then it is not (as Solomon implies in 2:31–33) because David’s house is innocent… but rather… because God’s grace is sufficient to deal with their guilt… The conditionality of the Davidic promise, then, is only part of the story… its unconditional aspects are also crucially important."
**Locus:** §3 / 1 Kgs 1–2 summary / slice ~l.176
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[solomon]], [[david]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R1-20
**Claim:** Provan rejects the neat early-good/late-bad bipartition of Solomon’s reign that starts reading at 3:4; 1:1–3:3 already undercuts easy correlation of Davidic-house obedience with Solomon’s established rule—establishment is more about God’s sovereignty than royal righteousness.
**Quote:** "that narrative—also about Solomon’s early days—is far from unambiguous in its assessment of the king’s actions after his accession to the throne and is quite unwilling to allow any easy correlation between the “obedience” of the house of David and the fact that David’s son now rules."
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3 (intro) / slice ~l.232
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]], [[davidic-covenant]]

### C-R1-21
**Claim:** Provan reads marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter (3:1) as criticism under Deuteronomy (17:16 return-to-Egypt; 7:3–4 intermarriage with ḥṯn)—the root of later apostasy already shown at the reign’s start.
**Quote:** "First Kings 3:1a cannot, therefore, represent anything other than a criticism of Solomon… We are shown right at the beginning of Solomon’s reign what the authors perceive to be the very root of his later apostasy (cf. 11:1–8)."
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3:1 / slice ~l.234
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-22
**Claim:** Provan takes 3:1b’s palace-before-temple order (against narrative chronology of chs. 6–7) as comment on priorities—palace more important than temple—and likely foreign-wife influence on divided loyalties.
**Quote:** "The order in which the projects are mentioned in 1 Kings 3:1b… is likely to be significant… a comment on the ordering of Solomon’s priorities; the palace was more important to him than the temple."
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3:1b / slice ~l.236
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-23
**Claim:** Provan relocates emphasis in 3:2 from exonerating the people for high-place worship to blaming Solomon’s delay in building the temple; high places remain potential disaster under Deut 12, later realized in 11:7–8, 33.
**Quote:** "it is much more probable in view of 3:1 that we should place the emphasis upon the second part of the verse, i.e., Solomon was to blame for the people’s continued worship at these places because of his delay in building the temple."
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3:2 / slice ~l.238
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-24
**Claim:** Provan heavily qualifies Solomon’s “love for the LORD” (3:3): unique for kings in Kings, yet surrounded by high-place statements and foreshadowing 11:1–2 loves of foreign women—love not wholehearted (not all heart/soul/strength, Deut 6:4).
**Quote:** "At the very least, then, the authors are again asking us to see… that Solomon’s love for God, even at this early stage in his career, was not entirely wholehearted… what kind of “love” is this, that does not issue in the keeping of the Law?"
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3:3 / slice ~ll.240–242
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-25
**Claim:** Provan on high places: always wrong for Kings’ authors relative to the one sanctuary of Deut 12; Solomon’s life patterns Judah later—toleration of YHWH-worship at high places then full apostasy.
**Quote:** "It is always wrong to worship at them, so far as the authors of Kgs. are concerned; it is particularly wrong when this worship becomes idolatrous. In this respect Solomon’s own life sets the pattern for what happens in the life of Judah later in the narrative."
**Locus:** §4 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 3:2 / slice ~l.268
**Targets:** [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-26
**Claim:** Provan reads Gibeon dream speech as Solomon’s limited theology (throne because David faithful/righteous), undermined by double ḥesed (“covenant love”) that recalls 2 Sam 7:15’s unconditional love even for a wrongdoing successor—God treated David unlike Saul though both sinned.
**Quote:** "The noun ḥesed, therefore, reminds us that even though Solomon is focusing upon conditionality, the nature of God’s dealings with the Davidic dynasty is unconditional."
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3:4–15 / slice ~l.244
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[david]]

### C-R1-27
**Claim:** Provan takes Solomon’s request for a discerning heart (not long life, wealth, or death of enemies) as recognition that ch. 2 “wisdom” was self-serving and must be replaced by wisdom for just rule; fear of the LORD as beginning of wisdom newly learned.
**Quote:** "The whole implication of all this is that Solomon has recognized and God is confirming that the “wisdom” of chapter 2 was of a highly unenlightened, self-serving sort, which must now be replaced with a higher sort, in order that the king may rule justly and well over his subjects."
**Locus:** §4 / 1 Kgs 3:7–14 / slice ~l.246
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-28
**Claim:** Provan distinguishes wisdom “from above” (supernatural gift in 3:4–15) from innate wisdom (implicit in 2:1–4) and patiently acquired observational wisdom (Proverbs; 1 Kgs 4:29–34).
**Quote:** "The emphasis of the line, and indeed of the whole section 3:4–15, is that this wisdom comes as a supernatural gift from God. It is not innate (as it is implicitly in 2:1–4); it is not acquired by patient hard work… This is wisdom from above, not below."
**Locus:** §4 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 3:12 / slice ~l.272
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-29
**Claim:** Provan notes conditional long-life promise (3:14) yet Solomon seems to have long life despite nonconformity—again law-and-grace question: does fulfillment depend on obedience or only involve it?
**Quote:** "Yet we shall see that Solomon apparently goes on to have a long life even though aspects of it are no more in conformity to God’s ways and statutes after this dream than they were beforehand. Once again, then, a question is asked about the relationship between law and grace."
**Locus:** §4 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 3:14 / slice ~l.276
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

**Claim:** Provan presents 3:16–28 as demonstrating that new God-given wisdom enables true distinguishing of right/wrong and justice after prior betrayal of justice in chs. 1–2; Solomon as model wise king of the wisdom literature.
**Quote:** "First Kings 3:16–28 now wishes us to see how the new wisdom he has just received from God makes all the difference in his ability to “distinguish between right and wrong” (3:9) and to administer justice (3:11)."

### C-R1-31
**Claim:** Provan flags the Hebrew of 3:27 (“Give the living baby to her”) as deliberately ambiguous for the reader—NIV’s “first woman” can mislead; darkness may place readers in Solomon’s position; sword now serves kingdom justice rather than ruthless self.
**Quote:** "There is nothing in the Hebrew text of 3:27, however, that implies this… Are the authors trying to put us in the same position as Solomon was in… His old “wisdom” had led to the use of the sword for executions whose justice is questionable. ### C-R1-32
**Claim:** Provan treats 4:1–20 as a unit (MT ch. 4): well-ordered, happy kingdom under God-gifted rule; Abiathar’s listing with Zadok may symbolize post-ch. 3 restoration and nullification of ch. 2 promotion—new order of God-given wisdom.
**Quote:** "This is a new order, an order devised out of God-given wisdom. It stands apart from the order based on the old wisdom of chapter 2. Nothing could symbolize this more clearly than the restoration of the banished Abiathar to the royal court."

**Quote:** "The authors clearly meant all Israel when they used the phrase in these chapters, and they meant this also in 4:7… It therefore seems apparent that the twelve district governors represented Solomon in all of Israel, including Judah."

**Claim:** Provan reads Solomon’s districts as a new order moving beyond the tribal system while retaining contact points—not a simple tribal tax system.
**Quote:** "Solomon’s arrangements thus move beyond the tribal system, while having points of contact with it. They represent a new order."

**Claim:** Provan links 4:20 happiness (eat/drink/happy; sand-on-seashore as Abrahamic Gen 22:17) to non-oppressive government and to 2:5–9’s ideal of Israel/Judah united at the king’s table (cf. 4:27).

### C-R1-42
**Claim:** Provan concludes Solomon’s “rule” over Hiram is real: cooperative treaty and reciprocal gifts (nṯn triad with God’s gift of wisdom), but Solomon ignores Hiram’s work-method terms (Israelites in Lebanon shifts; Gebal craftsmen)—senior/junior partnership, real beneficiary clearer later (9:10–10:29).
**Quote:** "Cooperation there may be, but it is cooperation between a senior partner and a junior who ultimately has no ability to resist his will."

### C-R1-43
**Claim:** Provan distinguishes forced labor groups: 30,000 Canaanite *mas* from “all Israel” (5:13–14; 9:15–23) vs 150,000 Israelites under foremen (5:15–18)—only the latter in view in 11:28 / 12:3–4; *mas* implies Canaanite corvée as in Joshua–Judges.

One comprises 30,000 Canaanites drawn from throughout Israel… The other comprises 150,000 Israelites… It is the latter group that is viewed in 1 Kgs. 11:28 and 12:3–4, a group that is never described by the word mas."

**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-44
**Claim:** Provan hears in 5:14 *bêtô* (“at home”) a possible allusion to Solomon’s palace: workers spend twice as much time on palace as temple even while temple work appears to press ahead (cf. 3:2; 7:1).
**Quote:** "If so, this must be another allusion to the royal palace (cf. 3:2). Even at this stage, the authors hint, Solomon is spending twice as much time on his palace as on the temple… while appearing to press ahead quickly with the latter."
**Locus:** §8 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 5:14 / slice ~l.514
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-45
**Claim:** Provan treats most architectural detail of ch. 6 as secondary for interpreting Kings; load-bearing is the word of God in 6:11–13: divine dwelling among the people remains conditioned on Law-obedience—temple does not change the divine-human relationship.
**Quote:** "God will certainly live among his people once it is built. But this “dwelling” will be on the same condition as before, namely obedience to the Law… For all its splendor, the temple does not change anything about the nature of the divine-human relationship (or, indeed, about the nature of God, cf. 1 Kgs. 8:27–30)."
**Locus:** §9 / 1 Kgs 6:1–13 / slice ~ll.532–534
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[davidic-covenant]]

### C-R1-46
**Claim:** Provan centers description on the Most Holy Place (ark, cherubim throne) and gold/fertility symbolism of carvings; temple took seven years (more precisely seven years six months, Ziv to Bul).
**Quote:** "It is not surprising, of course, that the inner sanctuary should attract such attention; this was the Most Holy Place… where the ark of the covenant was to be placed… Here the LORD sat, enthroned on the cherubim."
**Locus:** §9 / 1 Kgs 6:14–38 / slice ~ll.538–542
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-47
**Claim:** Provan rejects reading temple floral/cherubim symbolism as proof of original self-conscious syncretism; even if “Canaanite” forms, question is recontextualization claiming YHWH (not Baal/king) as fertility- and order-giver—warns against reductionist distrust of OT historical witness.
**Quote:** "What is not clear, however, is that the symbolism of the temple in general implies that it was from the start self-consciously syncretistic… Much depends here on the extent to which we are prepared to trust the witness of the OT texts to Israel’s history, rather than peering distrustfully behind them through reductionist spectacles."
**Locus:** §9 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 6:18 / slice ~l.564
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[solomon]]

### C-R1-48
**Claim:** Provan reads 6:38→7:1 word order/contrast (seven vs thirteen years; ḵlh + kol-bêtô) as authorial critique: palace prioritized and pushed to completion before temple fully finished—positioning of 7:1–12 between shell and furnishings itself narrates diverted energy.
**Quote:** "The implication is that Solomon not only spent more time on the palace project, but also pushed it through to completion before fully finishing his work on the temple. This explains why the account of the palace-building has been inserted between 6:38 and 7:13."
**Locus:** §10 / 1 Kgs 7:1–5 / slice ~ll.586–592
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-49
**Claim:** Provan holds the temple is not truly complete until interior work and worship (ḵlh in 7:40 Hiram; šlm in 7:51 Solomon)—until then “little more than an empty shell.”
**Quote:** "The temple is not really “complete” until all the work on its interior is finished and it is being worshiped in. This does not happen until 7:51… Until this point, the temple is little more than an empty shell."
**Locus:** §10 / 1 Kgs 7:1 / slice ~l.592
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-50
**Claim:** Provan presents Hiram/Huram the craftsman (Israelite mother, Tyrian father; Bezalel parallel in wisdom/understanding/knowledge) as carefully non-pure-Gentile; Solomon alone does gold work, Hiram bronze—spotlight remains on Solomon as preeminent wisdom embodiment.
**Quote:** "Hiram may himself be “full of wisdom and understanding and knowledge” and a worthy successor to Bezalel, but the authors are anxious that we should remember who is the preeminent embodiment of these qualities."
**Locus:** §11 / 1 Kgs 7:13–14, 48–51 / slice ~ll.620, 626
**Targets:** [[solomon]]

### C-R1-51
**Claim:** Provan links pillars Jakin (“he will establish,” ḵwn) and Boaz (possibly divine strength for the king) to dynastic hopes now bound up with the temple—God will establish the temple-builder’s throne as promised (2 Sam 7:13).
**Quote:** "A pillar named “he will establish” clearly implies that hopes for the future of the dynasty are now bound up with the temple. God will establish the throne of the temple builder, as he had promised (cf. 2 Sam. 7:13)."
**Locus:** §11 / 1 Kgs 7:15–22 / slice ~l.622
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-52
**Claim:** Provan on the bronze Sea: text leaves open pure symbolism (chaos subdued by creator YHWH) vs practical priestly washing (2 Chron 4:6; tabernacle basin parallels); stands/basins assumed practical; pots/shovels/sprinkling bowls for altar cleaning and sacrificial blood.
**Quote:** "It is not made clear in this passage whether its function was purely symbolic, representing the forces of chaos that have been subdued and brought to order by the LORD, who is creator of the world… or also practical."
**Locus:** §11 / 1 Kgs 7:23–47 / slice ~l.624
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-53
**Claim:** Provan frames temple beauty as designed to impress, yet 6:11–13’s obedience-condition is ominous: Kings will deconstruct Solomonic glory amid disobedience (plunder, stripping, destruction); beauty never guarantees God will not leave or judge (cf. Stephen, Acts 7; Luke 21:5–6; Ezek 10–11).
**Quote:** "that ominous word in 6:11–13 should prevent us from getting too carried away with the beauty of what we have seen. It reminds us that God is not half so impressed with structures as with obedience… In the Bible the beauty of temples is never any guarantee that God will not leave them or bring judgment upon them."
**Locus:** §11 / 1 Kgs 6–7 closing / slice ~l.628
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[solomon]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R1-54
**Claim:** Provan notes vague dating of ark transfer (8:1–2) vs precise 6:1, 37–38—consistent with delayed temple completion; timing at Tabernacles (temporary shelters/exodus memory) symbolizes move from temporary to permanent dwelling, which later generations misread as static YHWH tied to city/temple.
**Quote:** "Rather than seeing it as implying continuity between the new order and the old, they imagined that God had left the past behind—that the LORD was now a static deity tied to city and temple, bound to legitimate the status quo, rather than a dynamic deity free to move, bringing judgment upon sinfulness and oppression."
**Locus:** §12 / 1 Kgs 8:1–2 / slice ~l.652
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R1-55
**Claim:** Provan reads 8:9 (nothing in the ark but the two tablets) as applying not only to physical items but to God: ark witnesses covenant and real presence but cannot capture or define God; cloud/glory then confirms divine blessing on new worship arrangements (exodus/Sinai continuity).
**Quote:** "we are surely to take this as applying not only to other physical items, but also to God. The ark is witness to his covenant and symbol of his real presence. It cannot capture or define him."
**Locus:** §12 / 1 Kgs 8:3–13 / slice ~ll.654–656
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R1-56
**Claim:** Provan highlights Solomon’s “Name” theology (8:16–20; cf. 3:2; 5:3, 5): avoids saying God *lives* in the temple in a way that cancels transcendence—real presence and attention via the Name without collapsing immanence into captivity.
**Quote:** "One important feature of this speech… is the way in which the word Name is used as a way of avoiding saying that God actually dwells in the temple… God is not to be thought of as “living” there in any sense that detracts from the reality of God’s transcendence."
**Locus:** §12 / 1 Kgs 8:14–21 / slice ~l.658
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[davidic-covenant]]

### C-R1-57
**Claim:** Provan on “until this day” (8:8 and recurrent in Kings): for the ark phrase the “present” is earlier than final (exilic/postexilic) form—source survival or preexilic stratum; sometimes signals trustworthiness of received tradition rather than the final redactors’ present.
**Quote:** "the “present” that is in view is evidently an earlier one. The phrase must therefore represent in this instance a survival either from the source documents… or from an earlier (preexilic) version… Sometimes the phrase may not be intended by the final producers of Kings so much to make a claim about their present, as to make a claim about the trustworthiness of the earlier traditions."
**Locus:** §12 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 8:8 / slice ~l.682
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R1-58
**Claim:** Provan links Abiathar’s expulsion to fulfillment of the Shiloh word against Eli’s house (1 Sam 2:27–36), with Zadok as the “faithful priest”—Kings’ prophecy-fulfillment theme binding the book.
**Quote:** "The “faithful priest” who will “minister before my anointed one always” (1 Sam. 2:35), then, is Zadok (1 Kgs. 2:35). Kings is very interested in this idea of prophecy and fulfillment—one of the themes that binds the book together and gives it its distinctive atmosphere."
**Locus:** §3 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 2:27 / slice ~l.206
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[solomon]]

### C-R1-59
**Claim:** Provan (Add. Notes §1) reads Abishag’s commission language (ʿmḏ lipnê, sḵn, šḵḇ beḥêq) as sexually charged—courtiers seek active arousal of an elderly king, not mere nursing warmth.
**Quote:** "The courtiers thus seem to have in mind a heat more actively generated than would be the case if Abishag was simply lying beside David. That is why they look so carefully throughout Israel for such a beautiful girl."
**Locus:** §1 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 1:2 / slice ~ll.48–49
**Targets:** [[david]], [[succession-narrative]], [[kingship-in-israel]]

### C-R1-60
**Claim:** Provan notes name-pun construction in 1 Kgs 1: Haggith/ḥag (feast) vs Bathsheba/šeḇa–šḇʿ (oath)—while feast-son eats, oath-daughter activates the sworn word; literary predestination of the characters.
**Quote:** "While the son of the feast-lady eats, the daughter-of-the-oath reminds the king of what he has sworn… The story is constructed quite deliberately so as to make these connections between the mothers and their sons clear and to invest the characters with a sense of predestination."
**Locus:** §1 Add. Notes / 1 Kgs 1:41 / slice ~l.66
**Targets:** [[succession-narrative]], [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]]
